The logic of two workshops

When one workshop puts mechanics and paint under the same roof, it inevitably compromises: sanding and metal dust finds its way into spray booths, paint space competes with mechanical lifts, and technicians split between two crafts instead of mastering one. QSC chose complete separation — a maintenance facility with its diagnostic bays, mechanical zones and alignment station, and a painting facility with its controlled booths, color lab and chassis equipment — so each team works in the environment its craft demands.

What unites the facilities matters more than what separates them: the single QSC standard. Assessment before repair, a written scope before work, documentation after completion — you find them in both buildings alike. And when your car needs both, as after an accident requiring body repair followed by systems checks, the two teams coordinate the handover between them and you face one accountable QSC throughout.

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

Why does QSC run two separate workshops?

Because the two crafts conflict in one building: dust from mechanical work is the enemy of paint, and paint operations have no place beside engine repair. Separate facilities mean each team, space and set of equipment serves one discipline done properly.

Which workshop should I go to?

Engine, gearbox, electrical, AC, diagnostics, suspension or scheduled service → the maintenance workshop. Paint, dents, scratches, collision or body damage → the painting & bodywork workshop. Unsure? Call the main line and the team routes you.

Can one workshop move my car to the other if it needs both?

Yes — transfers between the facilities are handled by QSC with the same documented handover as any pickup, and you are kept informed at each step.
